newsitem.title: USA: Backlog of campus repairs at U.S. colleges soaring.
newsitem.headline: Backlog of campus repairs at U.S. colleges soaring.

text.p: America's aging college and university campuses need a whopping $26 billion in repairs, and $5.7 billion of that work is urgent, two leading higher education groups said on Wednesday.

The Association of Higher Education Facilities Officers and National Association of College and University Business Officers issued the warning in "A Foundation to Uphold," a report prepared with the aide of the Student Loan Marketing Association (Sallie Mae).
"Administrators are now maintaining aged buildings with outdated and failing systems," the groups said at a press briefing.
They said the average lifetime of the building materials at colleges is 23 years. Despite this, the average U.S. college building is approaching 40 years old, the groups said.
That means schools have "deferred maintenance" for an average 17 years, a level that threatens schools' ability to teach, the report says. And the backlog will only get worse, it said.

The report says public colleges delay repairs more than private schools and that research universities are the worst offenders. Research sites have over one-third of delayed repairs even though they are only eight percent of all higher ed institutions, the report says.
But the groups said some institutions are taking risks and finding innovative solutions, which often involve sale of bonds.

For instance, the University of Connecticut through its UConn 2000 project, persuaded the state legislature to fund $1.24 billion over the next 10 years using bonds. Also, the state will match all university-generated funds over $20 million.

After a careful audit of its funding needs, the Oregon System of Higher Education (OSHE) successfully appealed to the state legislature and won a 500 percent increase in maintenance funds since 1989, from $4.8 million biannually to $24 million, the report says.
The legislature increased funding through the state's general fund and a bond issue, the report says.

The report says Louisiana State University became a leader in renewing facilities when one of its projectss was named 1995 Project of the Year by the Association of Energy Engineers. The school is raising funds, in part, through a $50 million bond issue with debt-service paid by student fees.
And Jefferson County School District in Colorado cut its maintenance backlog by $200 million in four years through an "innovative" bond financing, the groups said.
